strengths: Well-motivated paradigm shift: Moving away from intermediate 2D-rendered pose maps (skeletons, depth maps, or rendered meshes) toward direct tokenization of raw 3D/4D motion sequences is conceptually elegant, avoiding pixel-level shape leakage and spatial misalignment.

Well-crafted technical pipeline: The combination of a 4D motion VQ-VAE (4DMoT), motion cross-attention in a DiT backbone, structured 4D RoPE (decomposing time and 3D spatial joint coordinates), and motion-aware CFG is coherent and well executed.

Strong empirical and qualitative performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results on the TikTok benchmark, demonstrating notable improvements in video-level FID and FVD, alongside visually appealing qualitative results across varied artistic styles and character proportions.

Thorough ablations: The ablation studies effectively dissect the design choices, validating the benefit of discrete vector quantization over continuous autoencoding, the necessity of 4D RoPE over 1D/3D or learnable variants, and the sensitivity of the motion CFG scale.
weaknesses: Backbone fairness and confounding factors: The model builds upon the 5B CogVideoX DiT backbone (~7B trainable parameters), whereas most competing baselines in Table 1 (e.g., AnimateAnyone, Champ, DisCo, MimicMotion) rely on 2D U-Net architectures (primarily SD 1.5, ~1B parameters). It is difficult to isolate how much of the quantitative boost (e.g., 65% drop in FID-VID) is due to the 4D motion tokenization versus the vastly superior generative capacity of the modern 5B DiT foundation model. An ablation comparing 4D motion tokens vs. 2D rendered pose conditioning under the exact same CogVideoX backbone would make the central claim much more compelling.

Limited quantitative benchmark diversity: Quantitative evaluation is restricted to sequences 335–340 of the TikTok dataset (only 6 evaluation sequences). Given that a core claim of the paper is robust handling of complex 3D motions and open-world generalization, quantitative evaluation or user studies on a broader benchmark (or challenging 3D motion datasets) are missing.

Ambiguity regarding multi-person animation: The paper repeatedly highlights support for multi-person animation in the Abstract, Introduction, and qualitative figures (e.g., Figure 14). However, in Appendix B under 'Single-person sub-clip extraction', the authors state that 'the current version of MTVCrafter cannot support multi-person animations with different poses.' Clarification is needed on how multi-character generation is technically supported and whether they are simply bound to synchronized identical poses.

Interpretation of 4D RoPE: As detailed in Algorithm 1, the spatial coordinates (x, y, z) for 4D RoPE use dataset-wide canonical mean joint coordinates rather than dynamic per-frame coordinates (since dynamic PE was shown to be unstable in Table 2). This essentially makes the spatial component a static anatomical joint layout embedding rather than full dynamic 4D coordinates; this design choice should be discussed and clarified more transparently in the main text.

strengths: Novel paradigm of directly quantizing raw 3D motion data (SMPL joints) into discrete 4D motion tokens, effectively avoiding the pixel-level geometric copying artifacts commonly observed in 2D skeleton- or depth-rendered animation pipelines.
Well-motivated integration into a modern Video DiT (CogVideoX-5B), utilizing cross-attention and a custom 4D RoPE design that combines temporal and 3D spatial coordinate encodings.
Efficient identity preservation via repeated concatenation of reference latents in the visual stream, avoiding the redundant compute and parameter overhead of maintaining a separate ReferenceNet.
Extensive qualitative demonstrations showing plausible transfer across a wide range of visual domains, including photorealistic humans, anime, 3D sculptures, and stylized illustrations.
weaknesses: Severely limited quantitative evaluation benchmark: The quantitative evaluation is conducted solely on a tiny subset of the TikTok dataset (only sequences 335 to 340, i.e., 6 video sequences). Given the claim of open-world animation and the scale of the base model, evaluation across larger and more varied benchmarks (e.g., UBC Fashion, in-the-wild benchmarks) or a comprehensive human perceptual study is noticeably missing.

Absence of pose accuracy metrics: All reported metrics (FID, FVD, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) assess image/video fidelity and low-level reconstruction, but none evaluate motion faithfulness or pose accuracy (e.g., Average Keypoint Distance (AKD), Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK), or Missing Keypoint Rate). It is difficult to verify whether the synthesized motions strictly adhere to the driving sequence.

Unfair baseline comparison due to model scale disparity: MTVCrafter builds upon CogVideoX-5B with ~7B trainable parameters, whereas most of the compared baselines (e.g., MimicMotion, AnimateAnyone, StableAnimator, ControlNeXt) are based on SD1.5 (under 1.5B parameters). The substantial leap in FID/FID-VID is largely influenced by the massive pre-trained video DiT backbone rather than solely the motion tokenization strategy.

Ambiguity in 4D RoPE formulation: As described in Algorithm 1 and Figure 11(b), the spatial RoPE coordinates are computed by subtracting the dataset-wide mean across all frames and joints, resulting in static spatial coordinates per joint. This means the spatial RoPE effectively acts as a static joint-ID rotary embedding rather than dynamically encoding the actual moving 3D coordinates over time, which partially contradicts the claim of dynamic 4D positional representation.

Inconsistent claims regarding multi-character generation: The abstract and introduction emphasize handling 'single or multiple characters', yet Section B of the Appendix explicitly acknowledges: 'Unfortunately, the current version of MTVCrafter cannot support multi-person animations with different poses.' Clarification on how multi-character references are processed or animated with a single SMPL sequence is needed.

strengths: Compelling Motivation and Paradigm Shift: Moving beyond traditional 2D-rendered pose maps (skeletons, depth, or mesh projections) to directly tokenizing raw 3D/4D motion sequences is a well-motivated direction. It mitigates rigid pixel-level copying and shape misalignment artifacts common in existing human image animation frameworks.

Effective Technical Components: The combination of a dedicated 4D motion tokenizer (4DMoT), 4D Rotary Positional Encoding (combining 1D temporal and 3D spatial priors), and motion-aware Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) provides a coherent and well-engineered framework for integrating structured motion into modern Diffusion Transformers (DiT).

Strong Empirical Results: MTVCrafter demonstrates substantial quantitative gains on the TikTok benchmark, significantly lowering FID-VID (6.98 vs. >20 for previous SOTA methods) and achieving competitive FVD. Qualitative results also show convincing generalization across diverse characters, non-human proportions, and artistic styles.

Informative Ablations: The ablation study systematically validates key design choices, clearly highlighting the benefits of vector quantization over continuous representations, the necessity of full 4D RoPE over 1D/3D or learnable variants, and the impact of the motion-aware CFG scale.
weaknesses: Lack of Explicit Pose Accuracy and Identity Metrics: The quantitative evaluation relies primarily on generative distribution metrics (FVD, FID-VID, FID) and pixel-level reconstruction metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). Standard evaluation metrics specifically assessing motion fidelity and pose tracking accuracy (e.g., Percentage of Correct Keypoints / PCK, mean joint position error) as well as identity preservation (e.g., DINO or face recognition cosine similarity) are missing.

Limited Evaluation Datasets: Quantitative evaluation is conducted exclusively on a small subset of the TikTok dataset (sequences 335 to 340). Evaluating on additional standard benchmarks (such as UBC Fashion or in-the-wild test sets) or conducting a structured user study would provide stronger evidence for the claimed open-world robustness.

Disentangling Backbone Capacity Gains: MTVCrafter builds on CogVideoX-5B (a ~7B parameter DiT framework), whereas many baselines (e.g., MagicAnimate, AnimateAnyone, MimicMotion, Champ) rely on smaller SD1.5 or SVD architectures. It is somewhat difficult to strictly isolate how much of the perceptual improvement stems from the larger DiT backbone versus the proposed 4D motion tokenization.

Dataset-Averaged 4D RoPE Formulation: According to Algorithm 1 and Section 3.2, the 3D spatial coordinates for RoPE are centralized using the global mean joint positions of the dataset rather than instance-specific kinematics. A clearer justification or ablation comparing dataset-mean spatial coordinates against dynamic per-instance coordinates would strengthen understanding of how well this handles dynamic or unconventional human postures.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated paradigm shift: Moving away from traditional 2D rendered skeleton/mesh guidance to direct tokenization of 4D joint coordinates (3D over time) conceptually solves the pixel-copying and body-shape misalignment issues common in existing character animation pipelines.

Strong zero-shot generalization across diverse morphologies: By learning motion tokens from differential joint coordinates decoupled from shape and camera projection, the framework demonstrates impressive animation transfer to non-standard body proportions, stylized characters, animals, and inanimate objects.

Thoughtful architectural formulation: The combination of a 4D motion VQ-VAE (4DMoT), motion-aware video DiT (MV-DiT), motion classifier-free guidance, and 4D rotary positional embeddings (4D RoPE) is well-designed and theoretically coherent.

Scalability across modern open-source backbones: The authors validate their method on both CogVideoX-5B and Wan-2.1-14B, showing that 4D motion tokens can be integrated cleanly into state-of-the-art large-scale video diffusion transformers.

Comprehensive ablations: The ablation studies (Tables 2 and 4, Figure 8, Figure 11) systematically examine critical components including discrete vs. continuous tokens, differential motion representations, codebook utilization, and various positional encoding designs.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative motion/pose alignment metrics: Evaluation relies primarily on standard image/video quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, FVD). For motion-driven animation, established pose fidelity metrics such as Average Keypoint Distance (AKD) or Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) are essential to verify how faithfully the generated characters adhere to the driving motion.

Unfair backbone advantages in benchmark comparisons: MTVCraft-18B is built on Wan-2.1-14B and MTVCraft-6B on CogVideoX-5B, whereas many compared baselines (e.g., ControlNeXt, Animate-X, MimicMotion) rely on older Stable Diffusion 1.5 backbones. While MTVCraft-6B does outperform UniAnimate-DiT and RealisDance-DiT, the substantial differences in underlying video generative capacity make it hard to strictly isolate the gains from 4D motion tokenization versus base model scale.

Missing subjective user evaluation: Given the perceptual nature of video generation and character retargeting, a user study evaluating identity preservation, motion faithfulness, and overall visual realism against leading methods is missing.

Clarification needed on 4D RoPE coordinates: For motion tokens, 4D RoPE utilizes dataset-wide mean joint positions rather than per-frame or per-sequence actual coordinates. A clearer justification and analysis of why static dataset-averaged positions perform better than dynamic frame-wise joint positions (beyond convergence speed) would strengthen the technical clarity.

Limitations regarding fine-grained articulated control: The reliance on standard 24 SMPL body joints excludes expressive hand and facial articulations, leading to visual artifacts or rigid hands in complex poses (as acknowledged in Appendix D).

strengths: Compelling conceptual shift: The paper addresses a core limitation of existing character animation methods—their reliance on 2D rendered pose images (e.g., skeletons, meshes, depth maps) that introduce rigid shape/appearance bias and discard 3D spatial depth—by proposing direct 4D motion tokenization from raw differential joint coordinates.

Well-designed technical architecture: The combination of 4DMoT (discrete differential joint tokenization via VQ-VAE) and MV-DiT with dedicated 4D RoPE (jointly encoding frame t and 3D spatial coordinates x, y, z) provides an elegant, principled way to inject 4D motion semantics into DiT models without pixel-level alignment constraints.

Comprehensive validation and strong results: The method achieves state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks (TikTok and Fashion) by large margins, particularly in generative video metrics like FVD (reduced from 402 to 276.65 on TikTok). The ablation studies systematically justify the necessity of quantization, differential representations, and the 4D RoPE design.

Scalability and impressive open-world generalization: The approach scales effectively from CogVideoX-5B to Wan-2.1-14B (18B total parameters), and exhibits remarkable zero-shot transfer capabilities across diverse visual styles, half-body compositions, non-human subjects, and inanimate objects.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation for out-of-domain / non-human generation: While qualitative visualizations on non-human characters and diverse artistic styles are very compelling, quantitative evaluation is limited to standard human dancing/fashion benchmarks (TikTok and Fashion). Including a dedicated user study or motion retargeting benchmark for non-human/open-world subjects would strengthen the claims.

Dependency on single-person 3D pose estimators: The driving condition pipeline relies entirely on SMPL fitting via NLF-Pose, inheriting its limitations (e.g., lack of fine-grained hand/finger articulation as discussed in Appendix D, inability to handle multi-person scenes, and potential tracking noise in complex camera motions).

Inference latency and computational profile: Although training details are clearly specified, the paper lacks a detailed analysis of inference cost (e.g., latency, FLOPs, or memory footprint) of 4D motion attention compared to conventional control modules like ControlNeXt or reference UNet/DiT architectures.

strengths: Conceptual novelty: Shifting from conventional 2D rendered pose images (which induce appearance and shape bias, unnatural pixel-copying artifacts, and lose depth cues) to directly tokenizing raw 4D motion sequences is an insightful and principled direction for character animation.

Well-motivated technical designs: The proposed 4DMoT elegantly decouples motion dynamics from subject shape by utilizing differential 3D joint coordinates. Furthermore, the 4D Rotary Position Embedding (4D RoPE) nicely bridges the spatial-temporal coordinates of motion tokens with the spatiotemporal tokens of video DiTs.

Demonstrated scalability: The framework is shown to be flexible across multiple foundation video DiT architectures and scales, including CogVideoX-5B and the recent large-scale Wan-2.1-14B, validating the generalizability of the motion conditioning scheme.
Strong empirical performance: MTVCraft outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods across standard metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, FVD, and FID-VID) on the TikTok and Fashion benchmarks.

Compelling zero-shot generalization: Without training on non-human datasets, the model demonstrates surprising emergent capabilities in transferring motion to diverse artistic styles, half-body characters, animals, and inanimate objects.
weaknesses: Upstream pose estimation dependency: The framework relies on off-the-shelf 3D pose estimators (e.g., NLF-Pose) to extract SMPL parameters. In cases of severe motion blur, extreme camera angles, heavy occlusions, or multi-person interaction, tracking failures or noisy joint estimations can directly bottleneck the animation quality.

Lack of quantitative evaluation for out-of-domain / non-human generation: While the qualitative results on animals and arbitrary characters are visually compelling, the paper lacks systematic quantitative evaluations, user studies, or pose alignment metrics specifically measuring non-human and stylized character transfer.

Limited fine-grained hand and facial control: Standard SMPL joint coordinates lack detailed hand articulation and expressive facial landmarks. As noted in the discussion, fine-grained hand and finger articulation remains challenging compared to methods leveraging dense whole-body keypoints or SMPL-X.
